forgiving you will help you reinforce the perception that it's okay for you to forgive
yourself. To forgive yourself, you only need to say, I forgive myself for using this story
that I have in my mind, this agreement I have in my mind, this image I have in my mind.
I forgive myself for using this story to abuse myself. I forgive myself for using
this image as an excuse to express anger to someone else.
You might even go to that someone and tell them what you're doing and saying, I'm practicing
forgiveness for myself.
And I'm asking you, will you please forgive me for using my story about you to abuse myself?
You're asking them to help you forgive yourself for abusing yourself.
My suggestion is that similar to the acceptance exercise,
where I had you say many times a day,
I accept life as it is,
even gave you a mala.
You can shift that now.
Certainly by now your awareness of what the judge is doing,
what the victim is doing,
and what the stories in your mind are doing
as far as creating emotional suffering are much higher.
Then the antidote to all that emotional poison running in the mind
in the mind is forgiveness.
And it's an emotional exercise.
You see, our very thinking about things,
which is mostly driven by the judge and victim in our mind,
our thinking about things will not get us out of
what our thinking has gotten us into.
What will get us out of it is action.
And the action that is the end to judgment and victimization
is forgiveness.
And you will need to practice it
more than just an intellectual exercise,
but you will need to practice it
with your words
and expressing it to yourself
and saying it out loud,
even if no one else is around.
That will help you
to undo and stop believing
the voices of the judge
and victim in your mind
that create emotional suffering.
In a mantra I share with people,
What I ask them to do is to forgive all the elements of their mind
and all the elements that played in their imagination
that created the emotional reaction.
And it's to be done with awareness of all those different elements
of our imagination and mind that dance and pull us into illusion
that we then have reactions from.
So the forgiveness mantra might sound something like this.
I forgive myself for not being what I expected myself to be.
And I forgive my mind for expecting me to be something I'm not.
And I forgive myself for trying to be what my mind said I should be.
And I forgive my judge for judging me for not being what my mind said I should be.
And I forgive the victim part of my personality for believing that that expectation was something that I should have been.
And I forgive my friend for not being what I expected her to be.
and I forgive myself for expecting her to be something she isn't.
And I forgive her for trying to be something she's not.
And I forgive her for expecting herself to be something she's not.
And I forgive myself for believing that expectation of her.
You see, there's a dance of the imagination.
And if we can forgive all those parts of the imagination that's created with our different archetype characters
that create all these images and pictures in our mind that create stories that we then believe,
it's more than just forgiving a person.
It's forgiving and letting go these stories and expectations that aren't true.
because so often it's not another person or ourselves
that have deceived us and betrayed us.
It's these myriad of expectations that run in our mind
that have deceived us,
and more specifically,
that we have deceived ourselves with,
that caused the emotional suffering.
This is where we can apply forgiveness
and start to really not believe
all the stories in our mind
and begin to see
life as it really is
without all those illusions.

13 Forgiveness Transcript

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/13-forgiveness/13-forgiveness-transcript

                                                                        May 12, 2019

What I wanna clarify about applying forgiveness is that it applies to “abuse”, and it
doesn’t apply to “knowledge”, and it should be a little clearer as we go through this
session. “Abuse” is where we create emotional suffering called “emotional abuse”. There
can also be a physical abuse. Oftentimes the emotional abuse and the residual pain from
it last a lot longer than the physical abuse. So, emotional abuse can be a lot more severe
and cause a long term suffering. While the physical body knows how to heal, the mind
doesn’t do it automatically – we have to move it along, and that’s where forgiveness
comes in.

Lets talk first about the process of “abuse”, so that we can know specifically where we’re
gonna apply this “medicine of forgiveness”. Hopefully, by now, it’s somewhat clear that
we really create the majority or all of our emotional suffering by ourselves. I just wanna
review for a minute how that happens and relate that to the impeccability, covered in
my friend Miguel’s book “The Four Agreements”. Let’s say there’s someone we work
with, and they agreed to finish a project by a certain day, or there’s our personal friend,
our personal relationship, and they agreed to have a meeting with us at a specific time.
But eventually it so happens that in either case they don’t meet their end of the
agreement. Then perhaps we become upset and get angry at them, or get judgmental
and critical of them for not meeting the agreed upon standards or the agreed upon
meeting time.

In the area of our stories we have a picture of what they were supposed to have done,
and that picture is confirmed by them having agreed to meet the agreed upon standard
or the agreed upon time. But then reality shows up and on that day things aren’t
delivered by them, or they don’t show up on the agreed upon time. This reality then is
not matching our expectations. And there’s a victimization there, because we haven’t
gotten in our reality what our imagination says we should have gotten, so there’s a
feeling of being cheated, created by the Victim’s story. Then there’s the unpleasant
emotional reaction to that story, and then there’s the judgment that we place upon that
person for causing us this emotional uncomfortableness, and we cast blame and fault
upon them, and then maybe our Villain comes at them with anger or resentment, or
maybe we judge ourselves with: “Oh, I should have expected that from them,” and we
kick ourselves and the Villain comes in and abuses ourselves for being so foolish to trust
them. In either case there’s some amount of punishment that the Judge calls for. This is
all about “abuse”, this is the abuse part of the story.

The factual part of the story, or what we call “the knowledge part of the story” is that: 1)
yes, you two had the agreement that they would deliver a product to you or that they
would meet you at a certain time, and that’s factual, and we could say you both agreed
on this set of criteria; 2) and the second fact is they didn’t then meet that criteria. And

                                                                                                                           1/10

that’s correct. But when we turn it into “right” and “wrong”, when we say we were right
and they were wrong, now we’re into a fault finding, abusive point of view and
expression. So, there’s the fact: “Yes, they agreed to this and then it wasn’t delivered,”
but then there are all the emotional interpretations that are abusive both to yourself and
to them.

Perhaps we’re waiting to meet somebody and they don’t show up. We’re feeling
disappointed or maybe we’re resentful, or upset with them for being late, and we’re
expressing that anger. They aren’t yet at the table, but our anger is coming out. We’re
thinking of them in our mind, and our anger is going towards them. At this point we are
to be aware of where that anger is really being received: while expressing our anger, we
have an image of them in our mind, and that image of them we have in our mind is
receiving the anger, while they aren’t even in the room. You see, our anger goes from
one part of our mind that’s expressing it to the other part of our mind that’s receiving it.

This receiving part is in a form of an image of them, but it’s still elsewhere in our own
mind and our anger is going to it. Now, perhaps that person shows up and we let her
have it by expressing our anger to her. What that person then does is they form a picture
of what they should be, they do the comparison and conclude that they are not what
they should be, and they feel ashamed or are angry at themselves, or somehow punish
themselves for not being what they should be, according to the archetypes in their mind.
Or perhaps they do nothing of it, because they know that they did the best that they
could. So, they may not feel abused at all by our anger, depending on how they form
their stories, their archetypes and their point of view. You see, our anger, our
disappointment or whatever we have, never actually gets to them. It may have the
impact, but it may not, depending on how their mind dreams images that they have and
how their Judge and Victim work. What’s important to notice is that we’re sending the
anger and we’re receiving the anger that we’re sending, and we’re feeling the anger that
we are sending. My friend Miguel would say that this expression is not impeccable.
Well, let’s understand a little more what that means. We could say that we’re the one
sending the anger and we’re the one that’s in emotional suffering because of all this
anger. We, not them, cause they may or may not be feeling that at all, depending on how
they interpret the situation.

We could say that this experience of anger is a “perfect justice”. And what I mean by
“perfect justice” is that while we’re holding them responsible and blaming them for our
anger, the truth is that we are the one that’s creating it, and we are the receiver of it. So
we express anger and we receive it. We could say that our expression is full of fault and
blame, and we could say that our expression is not impeccable. Let’s got back to the
meaning of “impeccable”. “Impeccable” means without sin, and I don’t mean this in a
religious connotation, but what I mean is “without fault or blame”. Well, our story is full
of fault and blame, so there’s a lot of sin. Fault and blame is an expression of the Judge
and of the Victim in our mind. Those two archetypes are expressing the fault and the
blame. The result of that is we’re expressing a lot of emotional poison, and we are also
receiving that emotional poison. Then, by making that not impeccable expression, that

                                                                                                                           2/10

fault and blame expression, we end up in emotional suffering, in emotional hell. And
how we ended up in this emotional hell of suffering is by creating and expressing the
fault and blame towards this other person. They don’t end up in hell, we end up in
emotional hell. And how long does it take? Instantaneously. As soon as we create the
anger, the judgment, the blame, and express it, we feel the experience of the judgment
and the anger. Then, going to hell because we sin happens immediately. It doesn’t
happen when our physical body dies. We don’t have to wait that long. If someone’s to
end up in emotional hell, they end up in emotional hell immediately as they commit the
sin of blame and fault. Then the price we pay for sinning, which is for not being
impeccable, is we suffer emotionally. It’s a perfect justice. Now, if this person that we’re
putting fault and blame on doesn’t believe our story about them, they don’t sin and they
don’t end up in hell. If they do believe the story we have about them, they create those
expressions in their own mind, by their own Judge’s and Victim’s expression about
themselves, and they create that emotional reaction, then they end up in emotional
suffering, which we can call “hell”. And the result is they sin by believing our story about
them. Did we create that? Not exactly, but we are certainly influencing the situation.
Are we responsible for what’s going on in their mind? Not in a way that we can control
it, but we certainly influence it. Are we responsible for what goes on in our mind?
Absolutely.

I clarify all this, because this is the abusive side of this interaction, the part that goes on
as the expression of the Judge and the Victim, and the images in the mind, that creates
the emotion. Did this person meet the agreement? No. But if our Judge and our Victim
get involved in the expression, this interaction turns into abuse, even if that abuse is just
for ourselves. It’s abusive. Would we be right by say: “Yes, they didn’t comply with the
agreement?” Yes, we’d be right, but we wouldn’t necessarily be happy. If we let our
Judge use the term “Hey, we were right, they were wrong,” – now we’re in the
judgment-victim interpretation. But if we have simply stated it as it is and said: “Ok,
they didn’t meet their end of the agreement,” – now it has less judgment and
victimization, and we have a chance to get away from some of the emotional abuse of
ourselves.

If we understand this situation, this framework, then we understand that forgiveness is
our story that we can start to apply to let go of the story of judgment and victimization.
Cause it’s those stories that are filled with sin that cause us emotional suffering. Then in
applying forgiveness, where do we need to apply forgiveness? We need to apply
forgiveness to the Abuser and to the Abused. Who are the Abuser and the Abused? The
Abuser is the Judge and the Villain in our mind, and the Abused is the Victim, even if
that Victim is the imaginary character we have of them, when we send them all the
abuse. We receive it as we send it, and we end up emotionally abusing ourselves with
our judgment and blame of someone else.

So, who needs to be forgiven? Us. Who needs to do the forgiving? Us. Then the forgiving
needs to be applied to our own mind. And why do we do it? Well, we apply it because we
don’t wanna suffer anymore. You see, as long as we continue with this story of the

                                                                                                                           3/10

Judge and the Victim, we keep sending our anger, our frustration, our disappointment
outward, and at the same time we keep experiencing it and receiving it. Then if the goal
is to be happy, we have to end this cycle. We can’t use the idea of “right” and “wrong” to
fix this. If we come in and say: “Ok, I see what I’m doing wrong and I’m gonna try and
stop doing this,” – now we’ve put a judgment on what we’re doing, we’ve found that
what we’re doing is wrong, and the natural conclusion of our mind from that dynamic is
to punish ourselves for having done something wrong. So we get angry at ourselves for
having done something wrong. Well, this is how we’ve been conditioned to stop doing
things. But this doesn’t change our dynamic. This is the Judge and the Victim in our
mind are now punishing ourselves, trying to get ourselves to stop punishing.

Well, more punishing of ourselves doesn’t keep us away from punishing ourselves. So,
what we have to do is jump tracks and switch the channel entirely. Then the new
channel is: “I forgive the Judge in my mind for making that expression and that
interpretation,” “I forgive the Victim in my mind for accepting the abuse of the Judge,”
“I forgive the Villain part of my mind for expressing all that anger, frustration,
disappointment,” and “I forgive those other images I have in my mind of this other
person for accepting all this abuse that my Villain sends,” – that’s the expression of
forgiveness. In this way we are the Forgiver, instead of the Abuser of these different
parts of our mind. And then we wanna play the receiver of forgiveness, and allow
ourselves to forgive ourselves and say: “Yes, I forgive myself for abusing myself with my
judgements, abusing myself with my Victim’s point of view,” “I forgive myself for
abusing myself with that Villain’s point of view and that Villain’s expression,” – now we
are allowing ourselves to receive our own forgiveness, on behalf of the Victim, the Judge
and the Villain.

You could say we’ve gone from the Abuser and the Abused archetype characters in our
mind to the Forgiver and the Forgiven. Then our point of view has changed, and the
story we tell from here on has changed. We are no longer abusing ourselves from the
point of view of Judge and Victim, we are forgiving ourselves and saying: “Yes, I did that
and I wish to do it no more,” “When I didn’t know what I was doing with all those
archetypes in my mind, I couldn’t have done any better than I did.”

If we keep forgiveness in the frame of whether there’s an abuse, whether there is
emotional unpleasantness and unhappiness, instead of whether somebody was right or
wrong, we can see where to apply it. It’s when we start to put forgiveness in terms of
“right” and “wrong” that we don’t apply forgiveness.

I was chatting with a woman after a talk I gave on forgiveness, and she was struggling
with it – she didn’t see how she could apply it. You see, she had been sexually assaulted
and she didn’t see any reason why this man should be forgiven, because he had really
hurt her, and she still, emotionally, had not recovered from this. And I asked her how
long it was, and it had been a few years. And I asked her if she was routinely and
regularly angry at him whenever she thought about him, and she was. What I shared
with her was that forgiving him wasn’t letting him off his responsibility for what he did.
It wasn’t saying that what he did was right, wasn’t condoning it anyway. Forgiving him
                                                                                                                           4/10

was a way for her to change the story she had about him, because as long as she kept the
story that “He was wrong”, “He shouldn’t have done that”, she was gonna feel like he
deserved to be punished more, which was gonna rationalize in her mind her anger
towards him. But she was the only one being abused with her anger. Her anger never
got to this man. She carried it around with her as she thought of him. Then, in her mind
she was right to be angry with him. She was right because he should be punished, and
the anger was her way of doing it. But she was the only one expressing anger, and she
was the only one receiving it. Then, in order to let go of that story, she had to see how
she was abusing herself with her anger towards this man. And it didn’t matter what he’d
done to her. Yes, he abused her one day 5 years ago, but she kept abusing herself day
after day for years. Then, the bigger abuse, the one that’s been lasting for years, has
been the abuse she’s been playing on herself about this man. To stop abusing herself any
longer, she had to forgive herself for being angry, for experiencing all that anger and for
receiving it on behalf of this man. Then she had to accept her own forgiveness and to
adopt a different story about this situation. The old story she was telling herself was
taking her to hell. Yes, it was the man who committed the crime, but she was taking
herself to hell with her judgments and victimizations of him. Well, the abuse was done,
the pain was inflicted, but for 5 years afterwards that was her half, her responsibility,
and it was nothing more, but self abuse.

As long as we hold the story that we were right, we will feel justified in expressing our
abuse, and we will be the one receiving it. And if we hold the story that we were wrong,
we will feel justified in accepting abuse from someone else or from our own Judge. In
either case, holding that story in the frame of “right” and “wrong” perpetuates the
abuse, because it continues to look for someone to punish. Then if we wanna get out of
the emotional suffering, we have to let go of the point of view of the Abused and the
Abuser, and to let go of the story of “right” and “wrong”, and of who deserves to be
punished and how much. Because as long as we’re holding that story, we’re abusing
ourselves. Then the story to adopt instead is “I forgive”: I forgive myself, I forgive all
those different parts of my mind that didn’t know what they were doing, and I forgive
that other person, not because they were right, not because I’m okay with what they did
now, but because I don’t wanna abuse myself anymore with the story I have about this
person. Or more precisely we might say: “I forgive them because I don’t want my Judge
and my Victim to abuse myself anymore with the story I have about this person.”
Forgiveness is about ending the emotional abuse, freeing ourselves from the Judge and
the Victim in our mind, cause we can’t do it by finding wrong what the Judge is doing,
by finding right what the Victim is doing. By finding what they are doing as “right” or
“wrong” we’re adding a Judge and Victim story on top of what the Judge and Victim are
doing, we jump back into that loop. Then forgiveness is a way to change that story. You
could say it’s the last chapter of the story, because after we forgive, there’s nothing more
to say about it.

One of the great resistances we have to forgiving is that we assume and imply that it
means something to do with “right” and “wrong”, that the person who was wrong
should ask for forgiveness, and the person who was right is the one that holds the power

                                                                                                                           5/10

of forgiving or not forgiving, as if being right were some reward. We don’t wanna ask for
forgiveness, because our mind implies that that means we were wrong, and if we were
wrong, then our Judge will judge us harshly, and our Victim will accept the abuse for
being wrong, and in order to avoid the pain of accepting that abuse we say: “No, no, I
wasn’t wrong, I’m not gonna ask for forgiveness.” This is the way we resist asking for
forgiveness, cause our mind is locked in that battle and doesn’t want to imply to itself
that it was wrong, because we’ll probably judge ourselves. This is one of the ways being
right leads us to be very unhappy. It’s when we can be humble that we have a greater
opportunity to be really happy. And being humble doesn’t mean you were wrong.
“Humble” isn’t about admitting you were wrong or being meek. “Humble” has more to
do with stepping away from a need to be right and a need to be wrong, and looking at
things with the point of view that it just was what it was, and that it ceases to be about
right and wrong, better or worse, and it becomes more important to be happy.

A lot of people assume that “humble” has to do with being weak. And I’ve come to see
“humble” as an incredibly powerful way of living, because humility allows us to live
without that self importance where we have to be right and find other people wrong, or
where we’re afraid of being wrong or afraid that other people will see us as wrong. It
unburdens ourselves from all those heavy standards and gives us an incredible number
of different options in which to live our life. To me that’s what humility is about.

If you wanna be happy in your life, you’ll forgive. And you’re gonna forgive the biggest
abuser in your life, which is your own belief system – that whole myriad of the mind,
that has the voice of the Judge, has the voice of the Victim. You’re gonna have to forgive
those two abusers. Just by doing this, you’ll be sitting in a point of view of watching
them, and just by doing that, you won’t be playing a role of Victim and you won’t be
playing a role of Judge, you’d be sitting in a neutral position, adopting a new story of
forgiveness, essentially saying: “I forgive myself for the way that Judge has treated me,
and I forgive the Judge for treating me that way, and I forgive the victim part of my
mind for accepting all that abuse on my behalf.”

Some people say: “I don’t know how to forgive.” That’s a lie. You know when we were
little kids and we were playing with our best friends in the same box or on the play
ground, and we got upset with each other, and the teacher came over and said: “Did you
mean to do that?” – “No, I didn’t,” or “Did they mean to do that?” – “No, they didn’t,”
“Well, if it was an accident, if it was something you didn’t intend to happen, then forgive
each other.” And we say: “Are you sorry?” “Yeah, we’re sorry,” “You forgive him?”, “Yes,
I forgive him.” We say: “I’m sorry,” and we say: “Yeah, I forgive you.” Because we fee
honest remorse of the pain we’ve caused or that our anger has caused. And then after
about 10 seconds we’re done, and we let go and we play with our friends again. So we
know from the very early on, naturally, how to forgive. And we do it so easily,
effortlessly, without resistance. But over the years we learnt how to really believe our
stories, really believe our Judge and really believe our Victim, and we invest in them
heavily, and we invest strongly in the idea that somebody should be punished. And we
believe that one of the ways to punish them is to continue to be angry at them. Of course

                                                                                                                           6/10

we’re the only one receiving our anger, but our mind says they deserve to be punished
with our anger, even though we’re still the only one receiving our anger, somehow
thinking we’re punishing them. I’m not sure why we would believe that, but we do. It’s
because we’ve become so invested in our story that we fail to see the common sense of it.
They blind us from seeing what we’re really doing with our emotions. We knew long ago
how to forgive. What we had to learn to do was to learn to hold on to our stories and to
not forgive – that’s what we learnt to do over years. Then once you start letting go of
your stories of “right” and “wrong”, and start with a new one and say: “You know what?
We did the best that we could, they did the best that they could, I did the best that I
could,” then we’re letting go of our stories, and forgiveness becomes a natural step.

Probably the biggest story that we hold on to is the one of expectation. It’s the one where
we have an image in our mind of what this person should have done, what the
circumstances should have come out to, or, in a case of self judgment, what weshould
have done. We make an agreement with ourselves of “I’m gonna do this”, and maybe we
fail and we judge ourselves for failing, but we hold that expectation in our mind. Or, in a
case of the person who we work with, that didn’t deliver the project on time, or a friend
who didn’t meet us on time, that expectation that they should have done that is
reinforced with their commitment to deliver or to show up in that time frame. Well,
their commitment makes that expectation in our mind much stronger. That story of that
expectation – that’s the one that we really have to let go of. Because it’s that expectation
that then becomes a basis for the judgment and the victimization story. We can say that
forgiving is letting go of that expectation story. A lot of times people make the act of
forgiveness and say: “I forgive you,” but when they think about that person later on, or
that instance later on, they have an emotional reaction. Well, the emotional reaction
comes because they’re still holding on to that image of expectation in their mind. If we
still have a self judgment from the past, it’s because we still have a self image or an
expectation of what we should have done, and whenever we think of that instance we
have that image of comparison that the Judge then assesses ourselves against and finds
us unworthy. You see, that image of expectation, whether that’s us or someone
else, that’s what we have to give up. Forgiveness means giving up that expectation and
saying: “You know what? They made that commitment with the best of intentions, or I
made that commitment with the best of intentions, but given the circumstances I didn’t
get to achieve, or that person didn’t deliver, based on what our imagination committed
to. Maybe it’s not that they failed the expectation, maybe our expectations weren’t
accurate, given all the circumstances.” Perhaps our Hero was the one that created that
image expectation of ourselves, or it’s our Princess archetype that made that image
expectation of someone else, or perhaps someone else who committed something to us,
it was their Hero archetype, or some other aspect of their personality that made that
commitment, based on what they thought they should be for us. And then it was
another one of their archetypes that they weren’t aware of that sabotaged delivery in the
way that they committed to. All parts of the agreements of their personality and
subconscious mind that they are not aware of, that they couldn’t overcome because they
didn’t know that those dynamics were in effect. Even if they made that commitment,
their subconscious mind can have other agreements that can sabotage that
                                                                                                                           7/10

commitment. Then it’s that expectation that’s to be given up. That’s the key element in
forgiveness – to let go of that expectation – similar to acceptance and making your
peace with life as it really is.

Sometimes when we have done something to someone (yelled at them, or have been
angry at them, or hurt someone, particularly a person that we care about) we often feel
like we don’t deserve to be forgiven. We have it in our mind that we did a really bad
thing and that we should be punished even more for what we did. In that case we hold
back from going and apologizing, and saying we’re sorry sometimes. And we certainly
won’t go ask for forgiveness because we don’t believe we deserve it. And even if someone
does forgive us, if they’ve made their peace with it, we may feel like they still judge us, or
we may know they don’t judge us, but we still judge ourselves. That’s because we have
the agreement that what we did was such a bad thing that we should still be punished,
and that we haven’t paid the punishment price yet. Well, according to our own Judge
and our own Victim, that price is never paid. The only time the price is paid is when we
forgive ourselves and say: “Ok, I did the best that I could there, and I don’t need to
punish myself anymore emotionally. The pain of inflicting that pain, the remorse of
inflicting that pain, was enough. There’s been enough pain created, and I’ve abused
myself enough for the pain created, and now it’s time to forgive myself.” You have to
just decide to do that, because your Judge and your Victim in your mind, will never tell
you when it’s time. The only time that that will happen is when you finally decide: “You
know what? It’s enough.” Your Judge and Victim will never let you off the hook. They
don’t know how. You have to decide. And you can do it any time.

And if someone else doesn’t wanna forgive you for what you’ve done, it doesn’t mean
you need to accept the abuse anymore. Yes, there could be an authentic feeling of
remorse, but it doesn’t mean you need to accept their abuse and still believe you need to
be punished. That’s the story in their mind, and that’s their Judge and their Victim
wanting to get the abuse out on someone else. Well, you can say that they are putting
themselves in their own hell, but you don’t have to go there with them. When we
understand that other people have reactions, and their Judge and their Victim have
stories in their mind that have taken control, and they are abusing other people with
their Judge and their Victim, or they are abusing themselves, then we can be aware of
that and say: “Wow, these people are really abusing themselves with their Judge and
their Victim in their mind.”

Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to give yourself the assignment of
forgiveness, to forgive the Judge in your mind a thousand times, to forgive the Victim in
your mind a thousand times, to accept on their behalf the forgiveness you’re giving a
thousand times. To play the role of forgiveness you need to forgive and accept that
forgiveness, so that you play the Forgiver and the Forgiven. And this is creating two
different points of view, you could say two new archetypes in your mind, that are
different from the judge and victim point of view archetypes. Then from these two new
points of view and these two archetypes, there’s no judgment and there’s no



                                                                                                                           8/10

victimization, which means there’s no fault and no blame, and there’s no creation of the
emotional suffering of hell. You’re finding a way to be impeccable from those two points
of view: the Forgiver and the Forgiven. This is an act of love for yourself.

Sometimes it’s difficult to forgive yourself when you don’t feel you deserve it. In those
cases you might go to someone, and apologize, and ask them to forgive you. Maybe they
don’t hold any grudge at all. But if you ask them and say: “Please forgive me for the pain
I’ve caused you,” then that face of someone who loves you and cares about you forgiving
you will help you reinforce the perception that it’s okay for you to forgive yourself. To
forgive yourself you only need to say: “I forgive myself for using this story that I have in
my mind, this agreement that I have in my mind, this image I have in my mind,” “I
forgive myself for using this story to abuse myself. I forgive myself for using this image
as an excuse to express anger to someone else.” You might even go to that someone and
tell them what you’re doing, and say: “I’m practicing forgiveness for myself and I’m
asking you: “Would you please forgive me for using my story about you to abuse
myself?”” – you’re asking them to help you forgive yourself for abusing yourself.

My suggestion is that similar to the “Acceptance” exercise, where I had you say many
times a day: “I accept life as it is,” even gave a mala. You can shift that now. Certainly by
now your awareness of what the Judge’s doing, of what the Victim’s doing, and what the
stories in your mind are doing to create the emotional suffering is much higher. Then
the antidote to all that emotional poison running in the mind is forgiveness. And it’s an
emotional exercise. You see, our very thinking about things, which is mostly driven by
the Judge and Victim in our mind, will not get us out of what it (our thinking) has got us
into. What will get us out of it is action, and the action that is the end to judgment and
victimization is forgiveness. And you will need to practice it not only as an intellectual
exercise, but you will need to practice it with your words, and expressing it to yourself
and saying it out loud, even if no one else is around. That will help you to undo and stop
believing the voices of the Judge and Victim in your mind that create emotional
suffering.

In a mantra I share with people, what I ask them to do is to forgive all the elements of
their mind and all the elements that play in their imagination that created an emotional
reaction. And it’s to be done with awareness of all those different elements of our
imagination and of our mind that dance and pull us into the illusion that we then have
reactions from. So the forgiveness mantra might sound something like this: “I forgive
myself for not being what I expected myself to be, and I forgive my mind for expecting
me to be something I’m not, and I forgive myself for trying to be what my mind said I
should be, and I forgive my Judge for judging me for not being what my mind said I
should be, and I forgive the Victim part of my personality for believing that expectation
was something that I should have been, and I forgive my friend for not being what I
expected her to be, and I forgive myself for expecting her to be something she isn’t, and
I forgive her for trying to be something she is not, and I forgive her for expecting herself
to be something she’s not, and I forgive myself for believing that expectation of her.”

You see, there is a dance of the imagination. And if we can forgive all those parts of the
                                                                                                                           9/10

imagination, with our different archetype characters that create all these images and
pictures in our mind, that create stories that we then believe, it’s more than just
forgiving a person, it’s forgiving and letting go of these stories and expectations that
aren’t true, because so often it’s not another person or ourselves that have deceived us
and betrayed us, but it’s these myriad of expectations that run around in our mind that
have deceived us, and more specifically that we have deceived ourselves with, that cause
the emotional suffering. This is where we can apply forgiveness, and start to really not
believe all the stories in our mind, and begin to see life as it really is, without all those
illusions.

13 Forgiveness

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/I9V7ptBc6uk

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Forgiveness lesson audio
You may want to listen multiple times.

2. Practice expressing forgiveness to Your Self. Use the expression of “giving up”
or “letting go” if you prefer. This exercise is about the commitment to release the
thoughts, emotions, and attitudes that cause you unhappiness.

3. Express forgiveness to your characters. Think of them as children lost in
dream or memory of the past. Some, like the Judge may have been mean to you. But
being mean back just continues the suffering. Forgiveness is an expression that breaks
the cycle.

4. Express forgiveness to others. This is so you can be relieved of the judgments,
criticisms, anger, resentment, and other painful emotions you have been carrying.

Some notes

The practice is about dropping the way you have been expressing emotions and words.
Dropping the expressions of rejection that cause you to repeatedly create unpleasant
emotions, and to create something different instead.

This is about your own healing, change, and happiness. It has to do with giving up the
stories you tell about yourself. It has to do with giving up the stories your characters tell
about you. It has to do with giving up the stories your characters tell about others.

Forgive all the parts of yourself for all those expressions, and you will lighten your
heart. If peace and happiness was going to be reached by judgment, resentment, or
carrying a grudge, we would have gotten there by now. Perhaps it is time to try

                                                                                                                                   1/5

something different for the sake of our own happiness.

Forgiveness for Expectations

I think one of the key elements that sets up an emotional reaction like disappointment,
hurt, resentment, or injustice etc, is the expectation. These expectations are often
invisible. Expectations are often the first domino in a chain of reactions. Once that is
crossed the victim is hurt, the judge has a right to criticize, and the villain can be angry.

Expectations get set up unconsciously by assumptions of characters and old beliefs.
Once the belief about expectation is accepted, then disappointment and hurt can easily
follow. However, if you see that the expectation didn’t fit with reality, then you can give
up the expectation. You can even forgive your past self for believing the expectation.
Give up the belief that it was a reasonable expectation, and the rest of the reactions fall
apart.

If I were to re-do the audio, I would spend more time explaining this first domino of
expectation. Forgive yourself for those past expectations. Forgive your past self for
believing in those expectations.

Then you will see differently your reactions when reality crashes them.

Resistance to change

Judge/Victim/Villain/Hero – I don’t want to forgive because that will mean that I am
letting them off the hook for what the did.

There is a belief here that the execution of punishment will free you from suffering.
These are two different things.

Let the justice or punishment system take its course. In cases you were wronged, then
pursue justice through that external path. But holding anger and resentment, and
criticism inside doesn’t punish anyone but yourself.

For the benefit of your mind, emotions, and soul, you will have to pursue an internal
path. The internal path of reaching justice, peace, or a settlement will require that you
give up your opinions, thoughts, and emotions.

This exercise is about you cleaning up the internal communication and emotions in
your mind. It is not about settling the score or debts outside. They are two separate
processes.

Even when there is an external settlement, you can still carry resentment, anger, and
painful emotions long after. The external settlement doesn’t automatically release your
internal feelings. If it doesn’t, then you will have to give them up yourself in a separate
process.



                                                                                                                                   2/5

The more you see this exercise solely about healing and changing your own emotions,
and thoughts, the less the resistance arguments will interfere.

Forgiving someone doesn’t mean that you then have to be friends or like them. One of
my clients, Jane, has a mother that was mentally ill. As a child her mother emotionally
and physically abused her. A long time ago Jane was advised by a therapist to cut off
contact. She cut off contact.

It took a couple years of work to forgive her mom for the neglect and abuse. In the
forgiveness of her mom, Jane did it without having any contact with her mom. It was
really a matter of Jane releasing all the emotions and judgments, and victim stories she
was carrying.

To this day, Jane still has no contact with her mom. She has a healthy boundary of no
contact. Jane feels completely differently, and is at peace with what she thinks about her
mom, but that doesn’t mean they have lunch or call her. Jane let go of all the negative
thoughts and emotions about her mom. After she did that, she still didn’t want
contact. These are separate things.

Because you forgive someone for something in the past, does not mean they are the kind
of person you want to subject yourself to. Know that you can still have a healthy
boundary of no contact after you give up your stories about them.

Common questions

What if I still hate what a person did to me?
Then you still hate. Begin with acknowledging where you are in the process. Acceptance
is an important part. It means not judging yourself for still having that hate.

Then practice some releasing emotions.

Write out what each of your characters have to say about that past event or that person.
Sometimes that hate is in there because those parts of you didn’t get to express what
they have been holding. If you let them speak into your journal, they can release what
they are holding as well. But this can only be released if you don’t believe what your
characters believe. Be empathetic with your past self that is hurt, but that doesn’t mean
add more faith to their stories.

When you allow those character parts to release the individual parts they are holding,
then you can let the overall feeling go. It may happen in a lot of smalls steps of
individual memories.

If you forgive someone, do you have to do it in person?
No. You don’t have to see or interact with someone to forgive them. Forgiveness is a
process that you do with your own beliefs, emotions, mind, and soul.

You can write a letter in order to express what you need to say, and then not send it.
                                                                                                                                   3/5

You can express on to paper, and then burn it in a fire. It is important for you to give up
what you are holding, but it doesn’t mean that the other person needs to be involved.

What if the other person doesn't deserve forgiveness?
Do you deserve to be free of the resentment, anger, and emotional hurts you are
carrying around?

That’s the question that matters here.

If you think that the anger and hurt in your emotional body is some how punishing
them, then I’d like to know how that works.

What if you feel you don't deserve to be forgiven?
The Judge will believe that you don’t forgiveness, or to be let off the hook. Even if he has
been berating the victim for 40 years about an event, it will still see the victim as not
deserving to be free of punishment.

The victim will also see it as not deserving to be forgiven. These two characters are stuck
in time still looking at you as if you were still the person of 40 years ago.

You will have to transcend the perspective of the Judge and Victim, etc, and see through
different eyes.

Perhaps you did something when you were 10 years old.

Remember back to who you were before you did that. You will see an innocent child.
The innocent child did something that didn’t know the consequences of, and couldn’t
help doing. They were a child.

Does that innocent child deserve forgiveness? Yes.

But once the child accepts the judgment, they are now masked. They are given a label of
being bad, terrible. They accept the emotions of shame and guilt.

That innocent is now turned into the victim with its painful emotions and identity. With
this new identity they do not deserve forgiveness. However, this is just a label about
one event. It is not their real identity. It is just a mask they are wearing over an innocent
child. 40 years later there is still an innocent child underneath the mask.

Forgiveness is about releasing the innocent child self from the victim / judge story that it
is still being punished in.

Afterwards it knew better, and can say, “I should have known better.” But before, it was
innocent.

If you see the person who did it as the victim, you believe you should have known better
But it was an innocent, naive child that did the deed. The one that didn’t know better.



                                                                                                                                   4/5

You can forgive her/him.

Supporting videos


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/4Gk603qlsLg

Sometimes injustice is real. People are really victimized. That doesn’t mean
we have to stay there.

Forgiveness is the way out of your own suffering that happens when you continue to live
in injustice.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/96oL56-0Fqk

Compassion is just large scale forgiveness for humans who you realize
are stuck in their emotional wounds.

Judgment leads to more rejection which leads to more pain. At a certain point you
decide to do differently because that is the only way to break the cycle.





                                                                                                                                   5/5
